survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 microdata for South Korea (15-year-old students) and applies a two-stage complex survey design in the underlying PISA sampling (schools sampled first, then students within schools). In the manuscript, the authors report listwise deletion to retain only students with complete responses to the learning-strategy items (N=3,310) and then conduct model comparison and subsequent correlation/quadratic regression analyses using plausible values for mathematics achievement. However, the paper does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the statistical analyses, nor does it name any weight variable (e.g., SENWGT_STU or TOTWGT). Because the analyses are based on IRT-based scoring and plausible-value procedures, analysts using the PISA international database should apply the appropriate student sampling weights and replicate weights if available, to obtain population-representative standard errors; the manuscript’s omission means the effective weighting strategy cannot be verified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2012 South Korea data. Because the student questionnaire uses a rotation design for the learning-strategy items, 33% of data for each learning-strategy item are missing by design; the authors then apply listwise deletion (complete-case approach) before analysis. From 5,033 participating South Korean students, only 3,310 students provided complete responses to the four learning-strategy items used in the study and were retained for analysis.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (South Korea, learning-strategy items scored with NRM; N=3,310)
main_findings.target_variable: Learning strategy score (NRM) vs GPCM model fit and reliability
main_findings.performance_metrics: NRM vs GPCM: LRT χ2[4]=215.008, p<0.001; AIC/BIC lower for NRM (AIC: 25,778.21 vs 25,985.22; BIC: 25,875.88 vs 26,085.47). Item fit: Q1 p-values >0.05 for all items under NRM; RMSEA <0.0125 for Items 2 and 3 (0.006 and 0.007), Item 4 RMSEA 0.014 (p=0.052). Empirical reliability: NRM 0.365 vs GPCM 0.214.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics data for South Korea, the study compared NRM and GPCM to create learning strategy scores, finding that NRM provided significantly better overall model fit (lower AIC/BIC; LRT p<.001) and higher empirical reliability than GPCM. This indicates that treating PISA learning-strategy categories as nominal (rather than ordered) can improve the measurement of learning-strategy use for subsequent achievement analyses, which supports more valid strategy–achievement interpretation in policy discussions.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (South Korea, learning-strategy score from NRM; N=3,310)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement correlation with learning strategy score (linear relationship)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Average correlation between learning strategy score (NRM) and mathematics achievement: ρ=0.18 (SE=0.00075), range 0.17–0.22; all correlations p<0.05.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics data for South Korea, the study leveraged the learning strategy score estimated with NRM to predict mathematics achievement, finding that the average correlation was positive (ρ=0.18, p<.05). This indicates that higher combined use of metacognitive strategies with memorization is associated with higher mathematics performance, suggesting that strategy-focused instructional guidance may be beneficial, while the study’s correlational design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (South Korea, learning-strategy score from NRM; N=3,310)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement quadratic relationship with learning strategy score (nonlinear relationship)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Quadratic regression: standardized quadratic coefficient β=-0.0667 (p<.001); unstandardized LS2 B=-5.168 (SE=1.496, 95% CI [-6.664, -3.672]); R2=0.03572. Model comparison: quadratic model better than linear (BIC 39,802 vs 39,807); quadratic better than cubic (BIC 39,808; cubic term not significant, average B3=-0.873, average p=0.46).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics data for South Korea, the study leveraged the NRM-based learning strategy score to predict mathematics achievement with a quadratic term, finding a significant negative quadratic association (β=-0.0667, p<.001) consistent with an inverted-U pattern. This indicates that the positive association between strategy use and achievement shows diminishing returns at higher strategy-score levels, implying that policy and practice should emphasize balanced, context-appropriate strategy use rather than maximizing strategy intensity.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2012 mathematics data for South Korea (analytic sample N=3,310) to examine how learning-strategy use relates to mathematics achievement. The authors first compare two IRT-based scoring models for four nominal learning-strategy items—NRM versus GPCM—using model fit indices (AIC/BIC, likelihood ratio test) and item-level fit (Q1, RMSEA), concluding that NRM fits better overall and yields higher empirical reliability (0.365 vs 0.214). For the achievement relationship, they use plausible values for mathematics and compute correlations and a quadratic regression between the NRM-based learning strategy score and mathematics achievement. The mean correlation is ρ=0.18 (p<.05), and the quadratic term is significantly negative (β=-0.0667, p<.001), indicating an inverted-U pattern with small effect size (R2=0.03572). Limitations include reliance on self-reported strategy items, listwise deletion after rotation-design missingness, and no explicit reporting of survey-weight application.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The study does not train predictive machine-learning algorithms; instead, it uses IRT-based nominal/ordinal response models (NRM/GPCM) to score learning strategies and then applies correlation and quadratic regression to study associations with mathematics achievement. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty (no supervised ML learners are evaluated), and the research design is classified as exploratory rather than predictive.
